summary:
Lampung province stands under Indonesia's national framework. The national penal code, signed in December 2022 and in force since 2 January 2026, punishes consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The same framework criminalises expression: the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment, and website and app blocks covering LGBTQ-related content remain in place. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option, and legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval. A trans visitor whose documents do not match their presentation can therefore be questioned on identity grounds at any point where papers are checked.

Provincial and district authorities add a layer of their own. OutRight International's study of discriminatory regional regulations examines eight Indonesian provinces, Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatera, South Sulawesi, South Sumatera and Yogyakarta, at both province and district level, and Lampung is named among them. The study documents regulatory restriction rather than a provincial criminal code: the sources do not set out which Lampung ordinances apply to visitors or what penalties they carry.

Trans people in Lampung have been targeted directly by the province's own enforcement machinery. In November 2018 the Satpol PP, the regional morals-and-order force, raided three trans women, detained them at the Satpol PP office and hosed them down at the firefighter building while an officer recorded the incident. The detention of trans people by that force, and the recording of it, indicates that identification as trans is itself treated as an administrative violation by provincial officers.

That incident sits inside a documented national pattern. A human-rights review records trans women murdered in 2017 in Bone, Semarang and South Sulawesi, and lobbying for anti-LGBT bylaws during election cycles from 2016 onward. A survey of 1,520 Indonesians carried out in November 2016 found that 16.6% of respondents held LGBT people in hatred. More recent national reporting ties rising vigilante violence against trans people to official condemnation, including a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat, and police raids on private gatherings continue, most recently the arrest of 75 people at a rented villa near Bogor on 22 June 2025.
tangentialFactors:
The regional regulation approach in Lampung differs in form from the two provinces that criminalise same-sex sexual activity outright, Aceh under provincial religious law and South Sumatra, whose punishments reach anyone present in the province including foreign visitors. Lampung is instead documented as a site of discriminatory bylaw-making and of administrative enforcement against trans people by a morals force.

Enforcement against trans people elsewhere in Indonesia has turned lethal in custody. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges, died in custody, and his mother alleges police beat him; Indonesian police denied that violence was used. Trans women were also murdered in 2017 in Bone, Semarang and South Sulawesi.

Public hostility has measurable backing. A November 2016 survey of 1,520 Indonesians found 16.6% hated LGBT people, and anti-LGBT bylaw lobbying has been reported from 2016 onward around election cycles. Reporting in August 2026 attributes a surge in mob attacks on transgender people to officials' public condemnations and to the October 2025 presidential decree placing LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy alongside separatism and terrorism.
localsOnly:
Residents of Lampung live under both layers: the national penal code provisions and the province's own regulations, alongside district-level rules examined in OutRight International's eight-province study. The Satpol PP, the regional morals-and-order force, operates directly against residents on the ground, as the November 2018 detention of three trans women shows.

Ordinary residents have no statutory protection against discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity at national level. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and identity documents carry only 'male' or 'female'.

Hostility expressed in surveys and bylaw lobbying is a domestic political condition rather than a visitor-specific risk: 16.6% of 1,520 respondents surveyed in November 2016 said they hated LGBT people, and anti-LGBT bylaw campaigns have run since 2016.
outOfScopeNotes:
The specific Lampung ordinances identified in OutRight International's study, their titles, their text and the penalties attached, are not reproduced in the sources available for this entry; the study names Lampung among eight provinces reviewed at province and district level but the underlying provisions remain to be verified against the local regulation texts.

No source states whether disciplinary or criminal proceedings followed the November 2018 Satpol PP action against the three trans women, or whether that force has conducted comparable operations in Lampung after 2018. The available record for the province stops at that incident.

Whether Lampung province has enacted any regulation addressing gender expression, venue licensing or public order against trans people since the 2022 study is not sourced here. Reporting on anti-trans violence and official hostility is national rather than provincial and cannot be attributed to Lampung specifically.
